newsitem.title: UK: Bombings in N.Ireland threaten peace process.
newsitem.headline: Bombings in N.Ireland threaten peace process.

text.p: Northern Ireland's two-year peace process lay in tatters on Tuesday after suspected Irish Republican guerrillas struck twice with bombs at the heart of the British army there, injuring 20 soldiers and 11 civilians.

Two car bombs, one placed to hit victims of the first being taken to an army medical centre, exploded at the Lisburn headquarters of the 18,000-strong British army force deployed as a deterrent against a quarter century of guerrilla warfare.

The attacks, an enormous breach of security certain to lead to a serious investigation by British security experts in the province, were the first such against a British target in Northern Ireland in more than two years.
And they raised fears among politicians and the province's 1.5 million people of a return to a 27-year conflict which has killed 3,200.

The first bomb exploded at the barracks in Lisburn in a car park in mid-afternoon and the second appeared to be designed to catch casualties being taken to the Army medical centre a short distance away.
The bombings caused immediate speculation of resumed retaliation by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas who killed 900 Catholics in a tit-for-tat war before calling a truce two years ago this month.
No group claimed responsibility for the attack but politicians, police and army suspected the Irish Republican Army (IRA) or one of its shadowy splinter groups.

"If anybody thinks, whether it is a splinter group or the Provisional IRA, that they can bomb the British Government out of the policy stance they think is right for Northern Ireland they are making a very serious and fundamental mistake," British Prime Minister John Major said.
His determination to press ahead with the peace talks, which have been in limbo virtually since their opening day, was matched by his Irish counterpart, Prime Minister John Bruton.

"This outrage, carried out without warning, is deliberately calculated to provoke further violence and bloodshed and is aimed at undermining the multi-party talks in Belfast," an Irish government statement said.

Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, said he regretted the injuries but argued that the bombing showed the need for his party to be included in faltering multi-party peace talks under way in Belfast since June.
In a statement to Irish media he said the blasts "emphasise the urgent need to fill the current protracted and dangerous vacuum with a process of real, inclusive dialogue."

Sinn Fein has been barred from the talks since the IRA resumed its war against British rule in February with attacks on the British mainland meant to pressure Prime Minister John Major into changing the ground rules for inclusion at the talks.

The past two years have been the most peaceful the province has known for a quarter of a century, allowing the army to retreat behind its barrack walls to give a semblance of normality to a province which has known only guerrilla war.

Major, who said that Northern Ireland was the most important item on his political agenda, was due to open his ruling Conservative Party's annual conference on Tuesday and was expected to face calls for a huge security crackdown.
Jailed Loyalists in the Maze prison were discussing whether to maintain a two-year truce by their activists still at large when the bombs went off within their hearing.

They are angry that the British government has failed to reward their ceasefire by freeing Loyalist prisoners. Britain says they are common criminals and there will be no amnesty for them or their Republican rivals.
